# Getting started

This page takes you from an empty project to a verified inclusion proof in a few minutes.

## Requirements

MerkleForge targets **Rust 1.97.1** or newer (edition 2024), the `rust-version` declared by every
crate. Check your toolchain with:

```bash
rustc --version
```

## Install

::::steps
### Create a project

```bash
cargo new merkle-hello
cd merkle-hello
```

### Add the crates

:::code-group
```bash [cargo add]
cargo add merkle-core merkleforge-hash merkle-variants
```

```toml [Cargo.toml]
[dependencies]
merkle-core = "0.4.1"
merkleforge-hash = "0.4.1"
merkle-variants = "0.4.1"
```
:::

Most applications want all three:

* `merkle-core` provides the traits (`MerkleTree`, `ProofVerifier`, `HashFunction`), the proof
  types, and `MerkleError`.
* `merkleforge-hash` provides the `Sha256`, `Keccak256`, and `Blake3` adapters.
* `merkle-variants` provides the trees.

Depend on `merkle-core` alone if you are writing your own tree or hash adapter.

### Write your first proof

Replace `src/main.rs` with:

```rust [src/main.rs]
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();

    tree.insert(b"alice:100")?;
    tree.insert(b"bob:250")?;
    tree.insert(b"carol:75")?;

    let root = tree.root().expect("tree is non-empty");
    println!("root: {root:02x?}");

    // Generate an inclusion proof for leaf 0 (alice).
    let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(0))?;
    println!("proof depth: {}", proof.depth());

    // Stateless verification: no tree needed, only the root, leaf bytes, and proof.
    let valid = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(root, b"alice:100", &proof);
    assert!(valid);

    // A different value for the same leaf is rejected.
    assert!(!BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(root, b"alice:999", &proof));
    Ok(())
}
```

### Run it

```bash
cargo run
```

You should see the root, then `proof depth: 2` (three leaves are padded to four, so the proof has
two sibling hashes).
::::

## What just happened?

1. Each `insert` hashed the raw bytes into a leaf, `H(0x00 ‖ data)`, and recomputed the path to
   the root.
2. `root()` returned the 32-byte commitment to all three leaves.
3. `generate_proof` collected the sibling hashes from leaf 0 up to the root.
4. `verify` rebuilt the root from `b"alice:100"` and those siblings, and compared it with the
   trusted root. It never touched the tree.

That last step is the **light-client pattern**: whoever holds a trusted root can check one value
without the dataset. The [Mental model](/docs/mental-model) page explains each piece.

## Build from many leaves at once

When you already have the full leaf set, `from_leaves` builds the tree in one `O(n)` pass. The
root, indices, and proofs are identical to sequential inserts.

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let rows = ["alice:100", "bob:250", "carol:75"];
    let batch = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(rows)?;

    let mut sequential = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
    for row in rows {
        sequential.insert(row.as_bytes())?;
    }

    assert_eq!(batch.root(), sequential.root());
    Ok(())
}
```

:::note
`BinaryMerkleTree::from_leaves` is new since 0.4.1 and listed under **Unreleased** in the
changelog. Use sequential `insert` calls if you depend on the published 0.4.1 crates.
:::

## Swap the hash function

Every tree is generic over its hash. Change one type parameter and nothing else:

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::{Blake3, Keccak256};

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let mut fast = BinaryMerkleTree::<Blake3>::new();
    let mut evm = BinaryMerkleTree::<Keccak256>::new();

    fast.insert(b"alice:100")?;
    evm.insert(b"alice:100")?;

    // Different algorithms, different roots.
    assert_ne!(fast.root(), evm.root());
    Ok(())
}
```

See [Hash functions](/docs/guides/hash-functions) for when to pick each one.

## Try the light-client example

The repository ships a runnable server/client split:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge.git
cd MerkleForge
cargo run -p merkle-variants --example light_client
```

```text
server: built tree and exported root + proof
client: tree dropped before verification
Stateless verification: true
```

The same flow runs in your browser on the [live demo](/demo).

## Next steps

* [Choosing a tree](/docs/guides/choosing-a-tree) when your data is a key-value map rather than a list.
* [Proofs & stateless verification](/docs/guides/proofs) to ship proofs to clients.
* [Serialization](/docs/guides/serialization) to store proofs and trees.

# Mental model

Think of a Merkle root as a **fingerprint for many values**. Change any value and the fingerprint
changes. A proof is the short path that lets another machine check one value against that
fingerprint.

## The four pieces

| Piece | What it is | In MerkleForge |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Leaf** | The hash of one value you inserted. | `H::hash(data)`, computed for you by `insert`. |
| **Root** | One digest that commits to every leaf. | `tree.root()` returns `Option<&H::Digest>`. |
| **Proof** | The sibling hashes on the path from one leaf to the root. | `MerkleProof<D>` (binary), `SparseMerkleProof<D>`, `MptProof<D>`. |
| **Verifier** | Code that rebuilds the root from a leaf and a proof. | `ProofVerifier::verify` and the per-tree `verify*` functions. |

```text
                 root = H(0x01 ‖ n01 ‖ n23)
                /                          \
     n01 = H(0x01 ‖ l0 ‖ l1)      n23 = H(0x01 ‖ l2 ‖ l3)
        /            \               /            \
 l0 = H(0x00‖a)  l1 = H(0x00‖b)  l2 = H(0x00‖c)  l3 = H(0x00‖d)
```

To prove `a` is leaf 0, the prover sends `l1` and `n23`. The verifier computes `l0` from `a`, then
`n01`, then the root, and compares it with the root it already trusts. For `n` leaves that is
`⌈log₂ n⌉` hashes, no matter how big the dataset is.

## Who holds what

* The **prover** (a server, indexer, or full node) holds the full tree. It publishes the root and
  answers proof requests.
* The **verifier** (a light client, browser, contract, or embedded device) holds only a **trusted
  root**, for example from a block header or a signed checkpoint.

A proof is only as good as the root you check it against. Get the root from a source you trust.

## Domain separation: `0x00` and `0x01`

MerkleForge hashes leaves and internal nodes in different **domains**:

| Hash | Pre-image |
| --- | --- |
| Leaf | `H(0x00 ‖ data)` |
| Internal node | `H(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right)` |

Without the prefixes, an internal node's pre-image (`left ‖ right`, 64 bytes) is also a valid leaf
value. An attacker could then present an internal node as if it were a leaf and forge a "proof"
for data that was never inserted. This is a **second-preimage attack**. With distinct prefixes, a
leaf hash can never equal an internal node hash for a different structure.

The `Sha256` and `Keccak256` adapters use the byte prefixes above. `Blake3` gets the same
separation from BLAKE3's `derive_key` mode with two context strings. See
[Hash functions](/docs/guides/hash-functions) for the exact constructions.

## Verifying by hand

Nothing in a proof is magic. This program rebuilds the root manually and checks it against the
library's own verifier:

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(["a", "b", "c", "d"])?;
    let root = *tree.root().expect("non-empty");
    let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(0))?;

    // 1. current = H(0x00 ‖ leaf)
    let mut current = Sha256::hash(b"a");
    // 2. Walk the siblings from the leaf level up to the root.
    for node in &proof.path {
        current = match node.side {
            ProofSide::Left => Sha256::hash_nodes(&node.hash, &current),
            ProofSide::Right => Sha256::hash_nodes(&current, &node.hash),
        };
    }
    // 3. Compare with the trusted root.
    assert_eq!(current, root);
    assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(&root, b"a", &proof));
    Ok(())
}
```

`ProofSide::Left` means the sibling sits on the left, so it goes first in the concatenation.

## Padding and empty slots

* `BinaryMerkleTree` pads the leaf layer to the next power of two with `H::empty()`, the hash of an
  empty leaf. Five leaves become eight slots.
* `SparseMerkleTree` has 2²⁵⁶ slots and precomputes the root of an empty subtree at every level,
  so empty regions cost nothing to store.
* `MerklePatriciaTrie` follows Ethereum's node layout and has no padding.

Because empty slots hash to `H::empty()`, **empty leaf data is rejected** with
`MerkleError::EmptyLeafData`; otherwise an inserted empty value would be indistinguishable from
padding.

## One caveat: `leaf_count` is not committed

`MerkleProof::leaf_count` tells the verifier how deep the path should be. The root does **not**
commit to it, so any count with the same padded size verifies. If the exact number of leaves matters
to you, get it from a trusted source and compare.

# Choosing a tree

MerkleForge ships three tree variants. They share the `MerkleTree<H>` trait but are built for
different shapes of data.

| | `BinaryMerkleTree<H>` | `SparseMerkleTree<H>` | `MerklePatriciaTrie<H>` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **Data shape** | Ordered list | Map from 32-byte keys to values | Map from byte keys to values |
| **Addressed by** | `LeafIndex` | `[u8; 32]` key | `&[u8]` key |
| **Proofs** | Inclusion | Membership and non-membership | Membership and non-membership (RLP witness) |
| **Proof size** | `⌈log₂ n⌉` siblings | 256 siblings, empty ones compressed to `None` | One RLP node per trie level on the path |
| **Best hash** | `Sha256` or `Blake3` | `Sha256` or `Blake3` | `Keccak256` for Ethereum roots |
| **Typical use** | Transaction batches, logs, file chunks, SPV | Account state, rollups, allowlists | Ethereum state, receipts, storage proofs |

## Quick decision guide

* **You have a list and prove items by position:** use
  [`BinaryMerkleTree`](/docs/guides/binary-merkle-tree). It has the smallest proofs and the fastest
  construction.
* **You have a key-value map and need to prove a key is absent:** use
  [`SparseMerkleTree`](/docs/guides/sparse-merkle-tree). Keys are 32 bytes, so hash longer keys
  first.
* **You need roots or witnesses that Ethereum tooling understands:** use
  [`MerklePatriciaTrie<Keccak256>`](/docs/guides/merkle-patricia-trie).

## Writing code that works with any variant

The shared trait lets you write generic code. Each variant also has a native API (keys for the
sparse tree and trie); the trait maps leaf indices onto it.

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::{BinaryMerkleTree, MerklePatriciaTrie, SparseMerkleTree};
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

/// Insert rows through the shared trait and return a metadata snapshot.
fn commit<H, T>(tree: &mut T, rows: &[&[u8]]) -> Result<TreeMetadata, MerkleError>
where
    H: HashFunction,
    T: MerkleTree<H>,
{
    for row in rows {
        tree.insert(row)?;
    }
    Ok(tree.metadata())
}

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let rows: &[&[u8]] = &[b"alice:100", b"bob:250", b"carol:75"];

    let binary = commit(&mut BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new(), rows)?;
    let sparse = commit(&mut SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new(), rows)?;
    let trie = commit(&mut MerklePatriciaTrie::<Sha256>::new(), rows)?;

    for meta in [binary, sparse, trie] {
        println!("{:<18} leaves={} height={}", meta.variant, meta.leaf_count, meta.height);
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

### How the trait maps onto each variant

* **Binary:** `insert` appends and returns the next `LeafIndex`. `remove` replaces the leaf with
  `H::empty()`; later indices are unchanged.
* **Sparse:** leaf index `i` is stored at a key whose last 8 bytes are `i` in big-endian order.
  `insert` returns the first unoccupied index at or above the leaf count, so it never overwrites a
  leaf after a removal. `generate_proof` returns a `MerkleProof` with 256 path nodes.
* **Patricia:** leaf index `i` is stored under the key `b"merkleforge:mpt:trait-leaf:" ‖ i`
  (8 bytes, big-endian). `generate_proof` through the trait returns
  `MerkleError::UnsupportedOperation`, because Patricia proofs are key-addressed. Use
  `MerklePatriciaTrie::generate_proof(key)` instead.

:::tip
Use the trait for generic plumbing (ingestion, metadata, benchmarks). Use each variant's native API
when you need key-addressed proofs.
:::

# Binary Merkle tree

`BinaryMerkleTree<H>` is a balanced binary tree over an ordered list of leaves. It stores leaves
and internal nodes in one flat, cache-friendly array, pads the leaf layer to a power of two, and
gives `O(log n)` inclusion proofs addressed by `LeafIndex`.

Use it for transaction batches, logs, file chunks, snapshot commitments, and Bitcoin-style SPV.

## Create a tree

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    // Empty tree, grows as you insert.
    let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
    assert!(tree.is_empty());
    assert_eq!(tree.root(), None);

    // Pre-size the leaf layer for at least 1,000 leaves (rounded up to 1,024).
    // Reserving storage adds no logical leaves.
    let reserved = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::with_capacity(1_000);
    assert_eq!(reserved.leaf_count(), 0);

    // Build from a known leaf set in one O(n) pass.
    let batch = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves([b"tx1".as_slice(), b"tx2", b"tx3"])?;
    assert_eq!(batch.leaf_count(), 3);

    tree.insert(b"tx1")?;
    tree.insert(b"tx2")?;
    tree.insert(b"tx3")?;
    assert_eq!(tree.root(), batch.root());
    Ok(())
}
```

`from_leaves` accepts anything that iterates over `AsRef<[u8]>`: `&str`, `&[u8]`, `Vec<u8>`,
`String`. It returns `MerkleError::EmptyLeafData` if any leaf is empty.

:::note
`from_leaves` is new since 0.4.1 (**Unreleased** in the changelog).
:::

## Insert and remove

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();

    // insert returns the stable index of the new leaf.
    let alice = tree.insert(b"alice:100")?;
    let bob = tree.insert(b"bob:250")?;
    let carol = tree.insert(b"carol:75")?;
    assert_eq!((alice, bob, carol), (LeafIndex(0), LeafIndex(1), LeafIndex(2)));
    assert_eq!(tree.height(), 3); // 3 leaves pad to 4 slots: 4 -> 2 -> 1

    // Removing an interior leaf replaces it with H::empty(); later indices stay put.
    tree.remove(bob)?;
    assert_eq!(tree.leaf_count(), 3);

    // Removing the last leaf shrinks the logical leaf count.
    tree.remove(carol)?;
    assert_eq!(tree.leaf_count(), 1);

    // Empty data is rejected so it can't be confused with padding.
    assert_eq!(tree.insert(b""), Err(MerkleError::EmptyLeafData));
    Ok(())
}
```

## Generate and verify proofs

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let txs = ["tx:alice->bob:100", "tx:bob->carol:50", "tx:carol->dave:25"];
    let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(txs)?;
    let root = tree.root().expect("non-empty");

    for (i, tx) in txs.iter().enumerate() {
        let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(i))?;
        assert_eq!(proof.leaf_index, LeafIndex(i));
        assert_eq!(proof.depth(), 2);
        assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(root, tx.as_bytes(), &proof));
    }

    // Out-of-range indices are an error, not a panic.
    assert_eq!(
        tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(9)).unwrap_err(),
        MerkleError::IndexOutOfBounds { index: 9, len: 3 },
    );
    Ok(())
}
```

`verify` is an associated function: it needs no tree instance. It returns `false` (never panics)
for empty leaf data, a wrong leaf, a tampered sibling, a path of the wrong length, or sides that
don't match the leaf index.

## Height and padding

| Leaves | Padded slots | `height()` | Proof depth |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 0 | 0 | 0 | – |
| 1 | 1 | 1 | 0 (trivial proof) |
| 2 | 2 | 2 | 1 |
| 3–4 | 4 | 3 | 2 |
| 5–8 | 8 | 4 | 3 |
| 1,000 | 1,024 | 11 | 10 |

A single-leaf tree has a **trivial** proof (`proof.is_trivial()`): the leaf hash is the root.

## Through the generic trait

`BinaryMerkleTree` implements both `MerkleTree<H>` and `ProofVerifier<H>`:

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Blake3;

fn verify_with<V: ProofVerifier<Blake3>>(
    root: &[u8; 32],
    leaf: &[u8],
    proof: &MerkleProof<[u8; 32]>,
) -> bool {
    V::verify(root, leaf, proof)
}

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Blake3>::new();
    MerkleTree::insert(&mut tree, b"leaf")?;
    let proof = MerkleTree::generate_proof(&tree, LeafIndex(0))?;
    let root = *MerkleTree::root(&tree).expect("non-empty");

    assert!(verify_with::<BinaryMerkleTree<Blake3>>(&root, b"leaf", &proof));
    Ok(())
}
```

## Clone, Debug, and serde

`BinaryMerkleTree` implements `Clone`, `Debug`, `Default`, `Serialize`, and `Deserialize`. The
serialized form stores only the hash algorithm name and the leaf hashes; internal nodes are
recomputed on load. See [Serialization](/docs/guides/serialization).

## Performance

On the reference machine (i7-1185G7), building a 100,000-leaf SHA-256 tree takes about 268 ms,
proof generation about 79 ns, and verification about 3 µs. See
[Benchmarks](/docs/performance/benchmarks) for the full tables.

# Sparse Merkle tree

`SparseMerkleTree<H>` models a fixed-depth **256-bit key space**: 2²⁵⁶ leaf slots, almost all
empty. It stores only non-empty nodes, precomputes the empty-subtree hash at every level, and
compresses single-leaf subtrees into shortcut nodes (Buterin, 2018) and small subtrees into batch
entries (Ouvrard, 2018/2019).

Use it for account state, key-value commitments, allowlists, and rollup state, especially when you
must prove that a key is **absent**.

## Keys and values

* A key is `[u8; 32]`. If your natural key is longer or variable-length (an address, a user ID),
  hash it to 32 bytes first.
* A value is any non-empty byte slice. The tree stores `H::hash(value)`.

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

/// Derive a 32-byte tree key from an arbitrary identifier.
fn key_for(id: &str) -> [u8; 32] {
    Sha256::hash(id.as_bytes())
}

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let mut state = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
    assert_eq!(state.root(), None); // root() is None while empty
    assert_eq!(state.depth(), 256);

    state.insert(key_for("alice"), b"balance:100")?;
    state.insert(key_for("bob"), b"balance:250")?;

    // Inserting an existing key overwrites its value.
    state.insert(key_for("alice"), b"balance:90")?;
    assert_eq!(state.leaf_count(), 2);

    // get() returns the stored leaf *hash*, not the value.
    assert_eq!(state.get(key_for("alice")), Some(&Sha256::hash(b"balance:90")));
    assert_eq!(state.get(key_for("carol")), None);

    state.remove(key_for("bob"))?;
    assert_eq!(state.leaf_count(), 1);
    Ok(())
}
```

`root()` returns `None` for an empty tree. If you need the canonical root of an empty tree (for
example as a genesis state), use `empty_root()`.

## Membership proofs

```rust
use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    let mut state = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
    let alice = [7_u8; 32];
    let bob = [9_u8; 32];

    state.insert(alice, b"balance:100")?;
    state.insert(bob, b"balance:250")?;

    let proof = state.generate_membership_proof(alice)?;
    let root = state.root().expect("state is not empty");

    assert!(proof.is_membership());
    assert_eq!(proof.siblings.len(), 256);

    // Checks the key, the value, and the path.
    assert!(SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_membership(
        root,
        alice,
        b"balance:100",
        &proof,
    ));
    // The same proof does not verify for another key or value.
    assert!(!SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_membership(root, bob, b"balance:100", &proof));
    assert!(!SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_membership(root, alice, b"balance:999", &proof));
    Ok(())
}
```

A `SparseMerkleProof<D>` has three public fields: `key`, `siblings` (256 entries ordered leaf to
root, with `None` for empty subtrees), and `leaf` (the stored leaf hash, or `None`).

:::warning
Use `verify_membership`, which checks that the proof is for the key you expect. The older
`SparseMerkleTree::verify` does **not** check the key and is deprecated.
:::

## Non-membership proofs

The same function proves absence. For a missing key, `generate_membership_proof` returns a proof
with `leaf: None`, and the verifier rebuilds the root with `H::empty()` in the leaf slot.

```rust
use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    let mut state = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
    state.insert([1_u8; 32], b"registered")?;

    let missing = [2_u8; 32];
    let proof = state.generate_membership_proof(missing)?;
    let root = state.root().expect("non-empty");

    assert!(proof.is_non_membership());
    assert!(SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_non_membership(root, missing, &proof));

    // A non-membership proof can't be replayed for a key that *is* present.
    let present = state.generate_membership_proof([1_u8; 32])?;
    assert!(!SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_non_membership(root, [1_u8; 32], &present));
    Ok(())
}
```

## Batch operations

`batch_insert` and `batch_remove` apply every change first, then recompute each affected node
once (one-phase batch update, Ma et al.). For many updates this is much faster than a loop of
single inserts.

```rust
use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    let mut batched = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
    let mut sequential = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();

    let updates: Vec<([u8; 32], Vec<u8>)> = (0_u8..100)
        .map(|i| ([i; 32], format!("account:{i}").into_bytes()))
        .collect();

    batched.batch_insert(&updates)?;
    for (key, value) in &updates {
        sequential.insert(*key, value)?;
    }
    assert_eq!(batched.root(), sequential.root());
    assert_eq!(batched.leaf_count(), 100);

    // Remove several keys in one pass. Every key must exist.
    batched.batch_remove(&[[0_u8; 32], [1_u8; 32], [2_u8; 32]])?;
    assert_eq!(batched.leaf_count(), 97);
    Ok(())
}
```

Rules:

* If a key appears more than once in `batch_insert`, the **last** value wins.
* `batch_insert` fails with `EmptyLeafData` if any value is empty, before changing the tree.
* `batch_remove` fails with `UnsupportedOperation` if any key is missing, before changing the tree.
* Single `remove` of a missing key also returns `UnsupportedOperation`.

In the published benchmark run (2026-08-17), a 1,000-key batch insert took 20.33 ms versus 8.69 s
for 1,000 sequential inserts. That run predates the **Unreleased** fix that makes single inserts
recompute only the changed path, so today's sequential numbers are far lower; batching still saves
work on shared ancestors. See [Benchmarks](/docs/performance/benchmarks).

## Empty hashes and storage introspection

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let mut tree = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();

    // Level 0 is the empty leaf; level 256 is the empty-tree root.
    assert_eq!(tree.empty_hash_at(0), &Sha256::empty());
    assert_eq!(tree.empty_root(), tree.empty_hash_at(256));
    assert_eq!(tree.empty_hashes().len(), 257);

    tree.insert([0xAB; 32], b"value")?;
    println!("materialized nodes: {}", tree.stored_node_count());
    println!("nodes written by last mutation: {}", tree.last_node_access_count());
    println!("estimate without batching: {}", tree.unbatched_node_count_estimate());
    Ok(())
}
```

The `merkle_variants::sparse` module also exports the constants `SPARSE_TREE_DEPTH` (256),
`EMPTY_HASH_LEVELS` (257), and `BATCH_DEPTH` (4), and the helper `bit_at(key, depth)` that
returns the path bit for a key at a depth (bit 0 is the high bit of `key[0]`).

## Through the generic trait

`SparseMerkleTree` implements `MerkleTree<H>` by mapping leaf index `i` to a key whose last 8 bytes
are `i` (big-endian). `MerkleTree::generate_proof` returns an ordinary `MerkleProof` with 256 path
nodes. Prefer the key-addressed API above for real state.

# Merkle Patricia trie

`MerklePatriciaTrie<H>` implements Ethereum's Merkle Patricia Trie (MPT): nibble-addressed byte
keys, four node types (empty, leaf, extension, branch), hex-prefix path encoding, RLP-encoded
nodes, and Ethereum's inline-or-hash node references.

With `Keccak256`, roots **match Ethereum**: the implementation is tested against the official
`trietest.json` and `trieanyorder.json` vectors from the Ethereum test suite.

## Insert, get, remove

```rust
use merkle_variants::MerklePatriciaTrie;
use merkleforge_hash::Keccak256;

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    let mut trie = MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::new();

    trie.insert(b"account:alice", b"100")?;
    trie.insert(b"account:bob", b"250")?;
    trie.insert(b"account:alice", b"90")?; // overwrite

    assert_eq!(trie.get(b"account:alice"), Some(b"90".as_slice()));
    assert_eq!(trie.get(b"account:carol"), None);
    assert_eq!(trie.leaf_count(), 2);

    // Removal collapses branches and extensions, so the root equals that of a
    // trie built from the remaining entries.
    trie.remove(b"account:bob")?;

    let mut fresh = MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::new();
    fresh.insert(b"account:alice", b"90")?;
    assert_eq!(trie.root(), fresh.root());
    Ok(())
}
```

Unlike the sparse tree, `get` returns the stored **value** bytes. Values must be non-empty
(`EmptyLeafData`), and removing a missing key returns `UnsupportedOperation`. `root()` is `None`
for an empty trie.

## Ethereum compatibility

The trie produces the same root as Ethereum clients for the same key-value set. This is the
`dogs` case from Ethereum's `trieanyorder.json`:

```rust
use merkle_variants::MerklePatriciaTrie;
use merkleforge_hash::Keccak256;

fn hex32(s: &str) -> [u8; 32] {
    let s = s.trim_start_matches("0x");
    let mut out = [0_u8; 32];
    for (i, byte) in out.iter_mut().enumerate() {
        *byte = u8::from_str_radix(&s[2 * i..2 * i + 2], 16).expect("valid hex");
    }
    out
}

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    let mut trie = MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::new();
    trie.insert(b"doe", b"reindeer")?;
    trie.insert(b"dog", b"puppy")?;
    trie.insert(b"dogglesworth", b"cat")?;

    let expected = hex32("0x8aad789dff2f538bca5d8ea56e8abe10f4c7ba3a5dea95fea4cd6e7c3a1168d3");
    assert_eq!(trie.root(), Some(&expected));
    Ok(())
}
```

Insertion order does not matter: the trie is canonical.

How compatibility works: the `Keccak256` adapter overrides `HashFunction::hash_encoded_node` to
return plain `Keccak-256(rlp)`, with no domain prefix, exactly as Ethereum hashes nodes. RLP already
distinguishes node types, so the `0x00`/`0x01` prefixes used by binary and sparse trees are not
needed here.

:::note
With `Sha256` or `Blake3` the trie works the same way but its roots are not Ethereum roots. A
custom adapter needs to override `hash_encoded_node` to produce Ethereum-compatible roots;
matching on the algorithm name no longer works (changed in **Unreleased**).
:::

## Witnesses (proofs)

`generate_proof(key)` returns an `MptProof<D>`: the key, the value (or `None`), and the
RLP-encoded nodes on the key's path, root first. It has the shape of an
[EIP-1186](https://eips.ethereum.org/EIPS/eip-1186) `accountProof` / `storageProof` entry.

```rust
use merkle_variants::{MerklePatriciaTrie, MptProof};
use merkleforge_hash::Keccak256;

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    let mut trie = MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::new();
    trie.insert(b"account:alice", b"100")?;
    trie.insert(b"account:bob", b"250")?;
    let root = *trie.root().expect("trie is not empty");

    // Membership
    let proof = trie.generate_proof(b"account:alice")?;
    assert!(proof.is_membership());
    assert_eq!(proof.value.as_deref(), Some(b"100".as_slice()));
    assert!(MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::verify_proof(&root, &proof));

    // Non-membership: the path ends at an empty slot or a divergent node.
    let absent = trie.generate_proof(b"account:carol")?;
    assert!(absent.is_non_membership());
    assert!(MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::verify_proof(&root, &absent));

    // A forged value fails verification.
    let forged: MptProof<[u8; 32]> = MptProof::new(
        proof.key.clone(),
        Some(b"1000000".to_vec()),
        proof.proof_nodes.clone(),
    );
    assert!(!MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::verify_proof(&root, &forged));
    Ok(())
}
```

`verify_proof` checks that the first node hashes to the trusted root, then walks the key's nibble
path through the witness. The verifier needs only the root and the proof, so it works for
light clients and cross-chain bridges. `MptProof` derives `Serialize` / `Deserialize`, so you can
send it over the network directly.

`generate_proof` on an empty trie returns `MerkleError::EmptyTree`.

## Low-level building blocks

The `merkle_variants::patricia` module exposes the encoding primitives for tooling and tests:

| Item | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| `NibblePath` | Byte key to 4-bit nibble path (`from_key`, `len`, `get`, `slice`, `common_prefix_len`) |
| `hp_encode` / `hp_decode` | Hex-prefix encoding for leaf and extension paths |
| `rlp_encode` / `rlp_decode` | RLP for `MptNode` values |
| `MptNode<D>` | `Empty`, `Leaf`, `Extension`, `Branch` |
| `NodeRef<D>` | `Hash(D)` for nodes ≥ 32 bytes of RLP, `Inline(Vec<u8>)` otherwise |
| `hash_node::<H>` | Ethereum-style reference for a node |
| `compute_root_hash::<H>` | Root digest for a root node (always hashed) |

```rust
use merkle_variants::patricia::{compute_root_hash, hp_encode, MptNode, NibblePath};
use merkleforge_hash::Keccak256;

fn main() {
    // The empty trie root, keccak256(rlp("")), well known from Ethereum.
    let empty = compute_root_hash::<Keccak256>(&MptNode::Empty);
    assert_eq!(empty[..4], [0x56, 0xe8, 0x1f, 0x17]);

    let path = NibblePath::from_key(b"key");
    assert_eq!(path.len(), 6); // two nibbles per byte

    // Hex-prefix flag for a leaf with an even-length path is 0x20.
    assert_eq!(hp_encode(&path, true)[0], 0x20);
}
```

## Through the generic trait

`MerklePatriciaTrie` implements `MerkleTree<H>`: leaf index `i` is stored under
`b"merkleforge:mpt:trait-leaf:" ‖ i` (8 bytes, big-endian). `MerkleTree::generate_proof` returns
`UnsupportedOperation` because Patricia proofs are key-addressed; call the inherent
`generate_proof(key)` instead.

# Hash functions

Every MerkleForge tree is generic over `H: HashFunction`. The hash decides the digest type, how
leaves and internal nodes are hashed, and what an empty slot looks like. Swapping it is a
type-level change: Rust monomorphises the generics, so there is no runtime dispatch.

## The adapters

`merkleforge-hash` ships three adapters. All produce `[u8; 32]` digests.

| Type | Algorithm | `algorithm_name()` | Best for |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Sha256` | SHA-256 | `"SHA-256"` | Interoperable binary and sparse trees; hardware SHA extensions |
| `Keccak256` | Keccak-256 | `"Keccak-256"` | Ethereum-compatible Patricia roots |
| `Blake3` | BLAKE3 | `"BLAKE3"` | Highest software throughput when Ethereum compatibility isn't needed |

```rust
use merkle_core::traits::HashFunction;
use merkleforge_hash::{Blake3, Keccak256, Sha256};

fn main() {
    let sha = Sha256::hash(b"alice:100");
    let keccak = Keccak256::hash(b"alice:100");
    let blake = Blake3::hash(b"alice:100");

    assert_eq!(sha.len(), 32);
    assert_ne!(sha, keccak);
    assert_ne!(sha, blake);

    assert_eq!(Blake3::algorithm_name(), "BLAKE3");
    assert_eq!(Blake3::digest_size(), 32);

    // Combine two child digests into a parent.
    let left = Blake3::hash(b"left leaf");
    let right = Blake3::hash(b"right leaf");
    let _parent = Blake3::hash_nodes(&left, &right);
}
```

`merkleforge_hash` re-exports `HashFunction`, so `use merkleforge_hash::HashFunction;` also works.

## Domain separation

| Adapter | Leaf: `hash(data)` | Internal node: `hash_nodes(l, r)` | Encoded node: `hash_encoded_node(rlp)` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `Sha256` | `SHA-256(0x00 ‖ data)` | `SHA-256(0x01 ‖ l ‖ r)` | `SHA-256(0x00 ‖ rlp)` (default) |
| `Keccak256` | `Keccak-256(0x00 ‖ data)` | `Keccak-256(0x01 ‖ l ‖ r)` | `Keccak-256(rlp)`, plain, Ethereum-compatible |
| `Blake3` | `derive_key("MerkleForge 2026 leaf v1", data)` | `derive_key("MerkleForge 2026 internal-node v1", l ‖ r)` | Same as leaf (default) |

`empty()` is the leaf hash of an empty slice, `hash(b"")`, for all three adapters. Binary trees pad
with it and sparse trees use it for vacant slots.

Why it matters: see [Mental model → Domain separation](/docs/mental-model#domain-separation-0x00-and-0x01).

```rust
use merkle_core::traits::HashFunction;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;
use sha2::{Digest, Sha256 as RawSha256};

fn main() {
    // The adapter's leaf hash is SHA-256 over 0x00 ‖ data.
    let mut raw = RawSha256::new();
    raw.update([0x00]);
    raw.update(b"alice:100");
    let expected: [u8; 32] = raw.finalize().into();

    assert_eq!(Sha256::hash(b"alice:100"), expected);
    assert_eq!(Sha256::empty(), Sha256::hash(b""));
}
```

(This snippet uses the [`sha2`](https://crates.io/crates/sha2) crate directly to show the
pre-image. You don't need it to use MerkleForge.)

## Choosing one

* **Ethereum interop:** `Keccak256`. Required for Patricia roots that match Ethereum.
* **Broad interoperability:** `Sha256`. Ubiquitous, and fast on CPUs with SHA extensions.
* **Raw speed:** `Blake3`. In the published run it hashed 1 MB at 5.99 GiB/s versus 1.28 GiB/s for
  SHA-256 and 291 MiB/s for Keccak-256. See [Benchmarks](/docs/performance/benchmarks).

A tree built with one hash can't be read with another: serialized trees store the algorithm
name and deserialization rejects a mismatch.

## The `HashFunction` trait

```rust
use core::fmt::Debug;

pub trait HashFunction: Send + Sync + 'static {
    type Digest: AsRef<[u8]> + Clone + Debug + PartialEq + Eq + Send + Sync + 'static;

    /// Leaf hash. Must apply the leaf domain, e.g. H(0x00 ‖ data).
    fn hash(data: &[u8]) -> Self::Digest;

    /// Parent of two children. Default: hash(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right).
    fn hash_nodes(left: &Self::Digest, right: &Self::Digest) -> Self::Digest {
        let mut buf = Vec::with_capacity(1 + left.as_ref().len() + right.as_ref().len());
        buf.push(0x01);
        buf.extend_from_slice(left.as_ref());
        buf.extend_from_slice(right.as_ref());
        Self::hash(&buf)
    }

    /// Hash of a self-describing encoding such as an RLP Patricia node. Default: hash(encoded).
    fn hash_encoded_node(encoded: &[u8]) -> Self::Digest {
        Self::hash(encoded)
    }

    /// Digest of an empty slot. Default: hash(&[]).
    fn empty() -> Self::Digest {
        Self::hash(&[])
    }

    fn algorithm_name() -> &'static str;
    fn digest_size() -> usize;
}
```

This mirrors the definition in `merkle_core::traits::hash_function` (doc comments shortened).

## Writing a custom adapter

Implement `hash`, `algorithm_name`, and `digest_size`. Apply the `0x00` leaf prefix in `hash`; the
default `hash_nodes` applies `0x01`. This example wraps the `sha2` crate's SHA-512/256:

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use sha2::{Digest, Sha512_256};

pub struct Sha512Trunc;

impl HashFunction for Sha512Trunc {
    type Digest = [u8; 32];

    fn hash(data: &[u8]) -> [u8; 32] {
        let mut hasher = Sha512_256::new();
        hasher.update([0x00]); // leaf domain
        hasher.update(data);
        hasher.finalize().into()
    }

    // hash_nodes, hash_encoded_node, and empty use the defaults.

    fn algorithm_name() -> &'static str {
        "SHA-512/256"
    }

    fn digest_size() -> usize {
        32
    }
}

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha512Trunc>::from_leaves(["a", "b", "c"])?;
    let root = tree.root().expect("non-empty");
    let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(2))?;
    assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha512Trunc>::verify(root, b"c", &proof));
    assert_eq!(tree.metadata().hash_algorithm, "SHA-512/256");
    Ok(())
}
```

Checklist for a custom adapter:

1. **Separate the domains.** `hash` must not collide with `hash_nodes` for different structures.
   Prefix leaves with `0x00`, or override both methods with your own separation (as `Blake3`
   does with context strings).
2. **Override for speed if you like.** `hash_nodes` can hash `0x01 ‖ l ‖ r` without the
   intermediate `Vec`, as the shipped adapters do. Keep the same output.
3. **Ethereum roots** need `hash_encoded_node` to return the plain hash of the RLP bytes.
4. **Use a unique `algorithm_name`.** Serialized trees store it to reject mismatched hashes.

:::warning
Since **Unreleased**, the default `hash_nodes` hashes `0x01 ‖ left ‖ right` instead of
`left ‖ right`. Custom adapters that relied on the old default now produce different roots.
The shipped adapters override `hash_nodes` and are unaffected.
:::

# Proofs & stateless verification

A MerkleForge proof lets a verifier check one value against a trusted root, with no access to the
tree. This is the property that makes Merkle trees useful for light clients, bridges, browsers, and
embedded devices.

## Proof types

| Tree | Proof type | Verify with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `BinaryMerkleTree` | `MerkleProof<D>` | `BinaryMerkleTree::<H>::verify(root, leaf, &proof)` |
| `SparseMerkleTree` | `SparseMerkleProof<D>` | `verify_membership(root, key, leaf, &proof)`, `verify_non_membership(root, key, &proof)` |
| `MerklePatriciaTrie` | `MptProof<D>` | `verify_proof(root, &proof)` |

The binary proof lives in `merkle-core`, so a verifier can depend on the shared types:

```rust
use merkle_core::types::{LeafIndex, ProofSide};

/// One step on the path: a sibling hash and the side it sits on.
pub struct ProofNode<D> {
    pub hash: D,
    pub side: ProofSide,
}

/// Inclusion proof for one leaf of a binary tree.
pub struct MerkleProof<D> {
    pub leaf_index: LeafIndex,
    pub leaf_count: usize,
    pub path: Vec<ProofNode<D>>, // O(log n) siblings, leaf level first
}
```

(Shown without derives and docs; `MerkleProof` also has `depth()` and `is_trivial()`.)

## The verification algorithm

```text
1. current = H(0x00 ‖ leaf_data)
2. for each node in proof.path:
     if node.side == Left:  current = H(0x01 ‖ node.hash ‖ current)
     if node.side == Right: current = H(0x01 ‖ current ‖ node.hash)
3. return current == expected_root
```

`BinaryMerkleTree::verify` also rejects proofs whose structure is inconsistent: empty leaf data,
`leaf_index >= leaf_count`, a path length that doesn't match the padded size, or sides that don't
match the bits of `leaf_index`. It returns `false` and never panics on malformed input.

## The `ProofVerifier` trait

```rust
use merkle_core::{traits::HashFunction, types::MerkleProof};

pub trait ProofVerifier<H: HashFunction> {
    fn verify(expected_root: &H::Digest, leaf_data: &[u8], proof: &MerkleProof<H::Digest>) -> bool;
}
```

It is separate from `MerkleTree` so it can be implemented by a type with no tree state at all.
`BinaryMerkleTree<H>` implements it, and its inherent `verify` delegates to it.

## Light-client example

The server builds the tree and exports the root and a serialized proof. The client receives bytes,
decodes the proof, and verifies, with the tree long gone.

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

/// What the server publishes: a root (e.g. in a block header) and proof bytes.
struct Published {
    root: [u8; 32],
    proof_bytes: Vec<u8>,
}

fn server(transactions: &[&str], index: usize) -> Result<Published, MerkleError> {
    let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(transactions)?;
    let root = *tree.root().ok_or(MerkleError::EmptyTree)?;
    let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(index))?;
    Ok(Published { root, proof_bytes: proof.to_bytes()? })
    // `tree` is dropped here.
}

fn client(trusted_root: &[u8; 32], claimed_tx: &str, proof_bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<bool, MerkleError> {
    let proof = MerkleProof::<[u8; 32]>::from_bytes(proof_bytes)?;
    Ok(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(trusted_root, claimed_tx.as_bytes(), &proof))
}

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let txs = ["tx:alice->bob:100", "tx:bob->carol:50", "tx:carol->dave:25"];
    let published = server(&txs, 0)?;

    println!("proof is {} bytes", published.proof_bytes.len());
    assert!(client(&published.root, "tx:alice->bob:100", &published.proof_bytes)?);
    assert!(!client(&published.root, "tx:alice->bob:1000", &published.proof_bytes)?);
    Ok(())
}
```

The repository ships the same flow as a runnable example:

```bash
cargo run -p merkle-variants --example light_client
```

Try it interactively on the [live demo](/demo): change the claimed value and watch verification
fail.

## What a verifier must trust

* **The root.** A proof only shows that a leaf is consistent with *some* root. Get the root from a
  trusted source: a block header, a signed checkpoint, a contract.
* **The leaf encoding.** Verify the exact bytes that were inserted. Agree on a canonical encoding
  (field order, separators, number formats) between prover and verifier.
* **Not `leaf_count`.** The binary root doesn't commit to `MerkleProof::leaf_count`. If the number
  of leaves matters, obtain it independently.
* **The key, for sparse proofs.** Use `verify_membership`, which checks the proof's key. The
  deprecated `SparseMerkleTree::verify` does not.

## Proof sizes

From the published comparison run on a 10,000-leaf tree:

| Library | Serialized proof size |
| --- | --- |
| MerkleForge | 469 bytes |
| `rs-merkle` | 448 bytes |
| `merkle_light` | 512 bytes |

A binary proof carries `⌈log₂ n⌉` 32-byte siblings plus a side tag each, the leaf index, and the
leaf count. See [Serialization](/docs/guides/serialization) for encoding options.

# Serialization

Proofs and trees implement `serde`'s `Serialize` and `Deserialize`. On top of that, `merkle-core`
provides the `Serializable` trait with compact binary helpers backed by
[`bincode`](https://crates.io/crates/bincode) 2 (standard config).

## The `Serializable` trait

```rust
use merkle_core::error::MerkleError;

pub trait Serializable: Sized {
    fn to_bytes(&self) -> Result<Vec<u8>, MerkleError>;
    fn from_bytes(bytes: &[u8]) -> Result<Self, MerkleError>;
    fn serialized_size(&self) -> Result<usize, MerkleError> {
        Ok(self.to_bytes()?.len())
    }
}
```

A blanket implementation covers **every** type that is `Serialize + DeserializeOwned`, so you
never implement it by hand. Errors map to `MerkleError::SerializationError` and
`MerkleError::DeserializationError`.

## Proofs

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(["alice", "bob", "carol", "dave"])?;
    let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(2))?;

    let bytes = proof.to_bytes()?;
    let recovered = MerkleProof::<[u8; 32]>::from_bytes(&bytes)?;
    assert_eq!(proof, recovered);
    println!("{} bytes", proof.serialized_size()?);

    // Garbage input is an error, not a panic.
    assert!(MerkleProof::<[u8; 32]>::from_bytes(b"not a proof").is_err());
    Ok(())
}
```

`SparseMerkleProof<D>` and `MptProof<D>` work the same way.

## Any serde format

Because the types are plain `serde` types, you can use JSON, CBOR, or anything else. With
[`serde_json`](https://crates.io/crates/serde_json):

```rust
use merkle_variants::{SparseMerkleTree, sparse::SparseMerkleProof};
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let mut state = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
    state.insert([7_u8; 32], b"balance:100")?;
    let proof = state.generate_membership_proof([7_u8; 32])?;

    let json = serde_json::to_string(&proof)?;
    let decoded: SparseMerkleProof<[u8; 32]> = serde_json::from_str(&json)?;
    assert_eq!(proof, decoded);
    Ok(())
}
```

:::tip
JSON encodes `[u8; 32]` as an array of numbers. If a browser or another language verifies your
proofs, define a small wire format with hex strings and convert at the boundary.
:::

## Trees

`BinaryMerkleTree`, `SparseMerkleTree`, and `MerklePatriciaTrie` serialize compactly. The encoding
stores only:

| Tree | Stored |
| --- | --- |
| `BinaryMerkleTree` | Hash algorithm name + leaf hashes |
| `SparseMerkleTree` | Hash algorithm name + `(key, leaf hash)` pairs in key order |
| `MerklePatriciaTrie` | Hash algorithm name + `(key, value)` entries in key order |

Internal nodes are **recomputed** on load, so a decoded tree is always internally consistent.
Deserialization rejects data written with a different hash algorithm.

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::{Blake3, Sha256};

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(["alice", "bob", "carol"])?;
    tree.remove(LeafIndex(1))?;

    let bytes = tree.to_bytes()?;
    let restored = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_bytes(&bytes)?;
    assert_eq!(restored.root(), tree.root());
    assert_eq!(restored.leaf_count(), tree.leaf_count());

    // Bytes from a SHA-256 tree can't be loaded as a BLAKE3 tree.
    assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Blake3>::from_bytes(&bytes).is_err());
    Ok(())
}
```

:::note
Tree `Serialize` / `Deserialize` (and `Clone` / `Debug`) are new since 0.4.1 and listed under
**Unreleased** in the changelog. Proof serialization is available in 0.4.1.
:::

## Metadata

`TreeMetadata` implements `Serialize` and `Deserialize`, but its string fields are
`&'static str`, so it can't be deserialized from an owned buffer and is **not** `Serializable`.
Serialize it for logs and dashboards, for example with `serde_json::to_string(&tree.metadata())`.
See [Metadata](/docs/guides/metadata).

# Metadata

Every tree returns a `TreeMetadata` snapshot through the `MerkleTree` trait. It is cheap to build
and useful for logging, dashboards, health checks, and benchmarks.

| Field | Type | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `leaf_count` | `usize` | Logical leaves stored |
| `height` | `usize` | `0` for an empty tree, `1` for a single leaf |
| `node_count` | `usize` | Allocated or materialized nodes (see below) |
| `hash_algorithm` | `&'static str` | `H::algorithm_name()`, e.g. `"SHA-256"` |
| `variant` | `&'static str` | `"BinaryMerkleTree"`, `"SparseMerkleTree"`, or `"MerklePatriciaTrie"` |

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(["a", "b", "c", "d", "e"])?;
    let metadata = tree.metadata();

    println!("variant: {}", metadata.variant);
    println!("algorithm: {}", metadata.hash_algorithm);
    println!("leaves: {}", metadata.leaf_count);
    println!("height: {}", metadata.height);
    println!("allocated nodes: {}", metadata.node_count);

    assert_eq!(metadata.variant, "BinaryMerkleTree");
    assert_eq!(metadata.hash_algorithm, "SHA-256");
    assert_eq!(metadata.leaf_count, 5);
    assert_eq!(metadata.height, 4); // 5 leaves pad to 8: 8 -> 4 -> 2 -> 1
    assert_eq!(metadata.node_count, 15); // 8 + 4 + 2 + 1
    Ok(())
}
```

`metadata()` is a trait method, so bring `MerkleTree` into scope (the prelude does).

## What `node_count` means per variant

* **Binary:** the length of the flat node array, padding included (`2 × capacity − 1`).
* **Sparse:** materialized storage entries (internal, shortcut, and batch nodes). Thanks to
  shortcut and batch compression this is far smaller than 256 per leaf. Compare with
  `stored_node_count()` and `unbatched_node_count_estimate()`.
* **Patricia:** materialized trie nodes, also available as `node_count()`.

## Serializing metadata

`TreeMetadata` implements `Serialize`, so you can log it as JSON:

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Blake3;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn std::error::Error>> {
    let mut tree = SparseMerkleTree::<Blake3>::new();
    tree.insert([1_u8; 32], b"value")?;

    let json = serde_json::to_string(&tree.metadata())?;
    assert!(json.contains("\"variant\":\"SparseMerkleTree\""));
    println!("{json}");
    Ok(())
}
```

Because its string fields are `&'static str`, `TreeMetadata` can't be deserialized from an owned
buffer. Treat it as output only.

# Errors

Every fallible MerkleForge API returns `Result<T, MerkleError>`. Verification functions return
`bool` instead: a bad proof is an expected outcome, not an error.

`MerkleError` lives in `merkle_core::error` (and the prelude). It implements `Debug`, `Clone`,
`PartialEq`, `Eq`, `Display`, and, with the default `std` feature, `std::error::Error`, so it works
with `?`, `Box<dyn Error>`, `anyhow`, and `thiserror`.

## Variants

| Variant | Raised when |
| --- | --- |
| `EmptyTree` | Proof generation (or binary `remove`) on a tree with no leaves |
| `IndexOutOfBounds { index, len }` | A `LeafIndex` past the last logical leaf |
| `InvalidProof` | Available to APIs that report failed verification as an error (the shipped verifiers return `false` instead) |
| `InvalidProofStructure(String)` | A proof's shape is inconsistent (e.g. sparse proof generation with a non-256 depth) |
| `EmptyLeafData` | Inserting an empty value (empty data would be indistinguishable from padding) |
| `SerializationError(String)` | `to_bytes` failed |
| `DeserializationError(String)` | `from_bytes` got malformed data |
| `HashError(String)` | An internal hashing step failed (for custom adapters; not raised by the shipped ones) |
| `UnsupportedOperation(&'static str)` | The variant can't do this, e.g. removing a missing sparse or Patricia key, or index-based Patricia proofs |
| `RlpError(String)` | Malformed RLP or hex-prefix data in the Patricia trie |

## Handling errors

`MerkleError` is `#[non_exhaustive]`: new variants may arrive in minor releases, so keep a
fallback arm.

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn describe(result: Result<MerkleProof<[u8; 32]>, MerkleError>) -> String {
    match result {
        Ok(proof) => format!("proof with {} siblings", proof.depth()),
        Err(MerkleError::EmptyTree) => "tree has no leaves".into(),
        Err(MerkleError::IndexOutOfBounds { index, len }) => {
            format!("leaf {index} is outside the current leaf count {len}")
        }
        Err(MerkleError::EmptyLeafData) => "empty leaves are rejected".into(),
        Err(other) => other.to_string(),
    }
}

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
    assert_eq!(describe(tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(0))), "tree has no leaves");

    tree.insert(b"alice")?;
    assert_eq!(
        describe(tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(3))),
        "leaf 3 is outside the current leaf count 1",
    );
    assert_eq!(describe(tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(0))), "proof with 0 siblings");
    Ok(())
}
```

## Display messages

```rust
use merkle_core::error::MerkleError;

fn main() {
    let err = MerkleError::IndexOutOfBounds { index: 5, len: 3 };
    assert_eq!(err.to_string(), "index 5 is out of bounds for a tree with 3 leaves");
    assert_eq!(MerkleError::EmptyLeafData.to_string(), "leaf data must not be empty");
}
```

## Using with `Box<dyn Error>`

```rust
use std::error::Error;

use merkle_variants::MerklePatriciaTrie;
use merkleforge_hash::Keccak256;

fn main() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> {
    let mut trie = MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::new();
    trie.insert(b"key", b"value")?;

    // Removing a key that isn't there is an error.
    let err = trie.remove(b"missing").unwrap_err();
    println!("{err}");
    Ok(())
}
```

# no_std

`merkle-core`, the crate with the traits, proof types, and errors, supports `no_std` targets with
a global allocator. That lets embedded devices, enclaves, and WebAssembly modules share proof types
with your servers and implement their own verifiers.

## Feature flags

| Feature | Default | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `std` | Yes | Standard-library integration, including `std::error::Error` for `MerkleError`. Implies `alloc`. |
| `alloc` | Via `std` | Heap-backed types (`Vec`, `String`) for `no_std` builds. Required. |

Disabling both is a compile error: proofs need `Vec`.

```toml [Cargo.toml]
[dependencies]
merkle-core = { version = "0.4.1", default-features = false, features = ["alloc"] }
```

Check a bare-metal build from the repository:

```bash
rustup target add thumbv7em-none-eabihf
cargo check -p merkle-core \
  --no-default-features \
  --features alloc \
  --target thumbv7em-none-eabihf
```

## What is available without `std`

Everything in `merkle-core`: `HashFunction`, `MerkleTree`, `ProofVerifier`, `Serializable`
(bincode), `MerkleProof`, `ProofNode`, `ProofSide`, `LeafIndex`, `NodeIndex`, `TreeMetadata`, and
`MerkleError` (without the `std::error::Error` impl).

:::warning
`merkleforge-hash` and `merkle-variants` currently depend on `merkle-core` with default features
and use `std` (the sparse tree uses `std::collections::HashMap`), so they are **std-only**. On a
`no_std` target, depend on `merkle-core` alone and supply a `HashFunction` adapter and verifier.
:::

## A no_std verifier

This verifier uses only `merkle-core` types and `core`, so it compiles in a `#![no_std]` crate with
`alloc`. It follows the same algorithm as `BinaryMerkleTree::verify`. Shown here with a host-side
`main` that cross-checks it against the real tree:

```rust
use merkle_core::{
    traits::HashFunction,
    types::{MerkleProof, ProofSide},
};

/// Stateless binary-proof check using only merkle-core.
pub fn verify_binary<H: HashFunction>(
    expected_root: &H::Digest,
    leaf_data: &[u8],
    proof: &MerkleProof<H::Digest>,
) -> bool {
    if leaf_data.is_empty() || proof.leaf_index.value() >= proof.leaf_count {
        return false;
    }
    let Some(capacity) = proof.leaf_count.checked_next_power_of_two() else {
        return false;
    };
    if proof.path.len() != capacity.ilog2() as usize {
        return false;
    }

    let mut current = H::hash(leaf_data);
    let mut offset = proof.leaf_index.value();
    for node in &proof.path {
        let expected = if offset % 2 == 0 { ProofSide::Right } else { ProofSide::Left };
        if node.side != expected {
            return false;
        }
        current = match node.side {
            ProofSide::Left => H::hash_nodes(&node.hash, &current),
            ProofSide::Right => H::hash_nodes(&current, &node.hash),
        };
        offset /= 2;
    }
    current == *expected_root
}

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    use merkle_core::types::LeafIndex;
    use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
    use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

    let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(["a", "b", "c"])?;
    let root = tree.root().expect("non-empty");
    let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(2))?;
    assert!(verify_binary::<Sha256>(root, b"c", &proof));
    assert!(!verify_binary::<Sha256>(root, b"x", &proof));
    Ok(())
}
```

On the device, provide a `HashFunction` implementation backed by a `no_std` hash crate (for
example `sha2` with `default-features = false`), following the
[custom adapter guide](/docs/guides/hash-functions#writing-a-custom-adapter).

# Benchmarks

MerkleForge uses [Criterion](https://crates.io/crates/criterion) benchmarks in the unpublished
`merkle-bench` crate to compare hash adapters, tree variants, proof generation, proof
verification, and other Rust Merkle libraries. Criterion reports mean, median, and standard
deviation to filter out noise.

Lower latency is better; higher throughput is better. For the latest CI numbers with links to every
Criterion report, see the [live benchmark explorer](/benchmarks).

:::note
The tables below are copied from [`BENCHMARKS.md`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/blob/main/BENCHMARKS.md)
(run date 2026-08-17). That run predates the **Unreleased** sparse-tree and Patricia-trie
performance fixes, which cut 4,000 sequential sparse inserts from about 223 s to 0.2 s and
4,000 Patricia inserts from about 5.9 s to 0.02 s. Sparse and Patricia numbers here are therefore
pessimistic. Cells marked *not captured* were not completed in that run.
:::

## Environment

| | |
| --- | --- |
| CPU | 11th Gen Intel Core i7-1185G7 @ 3.00 GHz, 4 cores / 8 threads, x86_64 |
| RAM | 15 GiB |
| OS | Linux 7.0.0-28-generic x86_64 |
| Rust | rustc 1.97.1 (8bab26f4f 2026-07-14) |
| Date | 2026-08-17 |

## Hash function throughput

`cargo bench --bench hash_throughput`

| Algorithm | 32 B latency | 64 B latency | 1 MB throughput |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SHA-256 | 109.60 ns | 177.40 ns | 1.28 GiB/s |
| Keccak-256 | 1.23 µs | 660.99 ns | 291.12 MiB/s |
| BLAKE3 | 230.70 ns | 247.83 ns | 5.99 GiB/s |

## Binary Merkle tree

`cargo bench --bench binary_tree`

| Leaves | Construction (SHA-256) | Construction (BLAKE3) | Proof gen | Proof verify |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 100 | 147.19 µs | 140.96 µs | 45.22 ns | 1.09 µs |
| 1,000 | 1.80 ms | 1.83 ms | 57.21 ns | 1.87 µs |
| 10,000 | 30.53 ms | 39.07 ms | 74.18 ns | 2.06 µs |
| 100,000 | 268.23 ms | 274.93 ms | 78.69 ns | 2.95 µs |

Construction builds a fresh `BinaryMerkleTree<H>`. Proof generation uses `LeafIndex(0)`. Proof
verification checks the proof against the recorded root and the original leaf bytes.

## Sparse Merkle tree

`cargo bench --bench sparse_tree` (SHA-256)

| Existing keys | Insert | Proof gen | Proof verify | Non-membership proof | Non-membership verify |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | 189.85 µs | 244.18 µs | 91.43 µs | 268.20 µs | 74.38 µs |
| 100 | 2.11 ms | 2.25 ms | 75.74 µs | 2.32 ms | 76.86 µs |
| 1,000 | 20.24 ms | 20.32 ms | 81.58 µs | 20.12 ms | 71.28 µs |
| 10,000 | 181.05 ms | 198.84 ms | 63.00 µs | 203.49 ms | 76.41 µs |

### Batch updates

| Batch size | Batch insert | Sequential insert | Speedup |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | 288.97 µs | 1.53 ms | 5.30× |
| 100 | 2.08 ms | 88.12 ms | 42.46× |
| 1,000 | 20.33 ms | 8.69 s | 427.72× |

## Merkle Patricia trie

`cargo bench --bench patricia_trie` (Keccak-256)

| Existing entries | Insert | Get | Proof gen | Proof verify |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10 | 20.61 µs | 159.00 ns | not captured | not captured |
| 100 | 217.63 µs | 200.07 ns | not captured | not captured |
| 1,000 | 2.11 ms | 270.26 ns | not captured | not captured |
| 10,000 | not captured | 387.44 ns | not captured | not captured |

State-root timings (`patricia_trie/state_root`) were not captured in this run.

## Energy-aware construction

`cargo bench --bench bench_energy` builds a 100,000-leaf binary tree.

| Algorithm | 100K construction time | CPU cycles | Package energy |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| SHA-256 | 463.52 ms | not captured | not captured |
| Keccak-256 | 1.49 s | not captured | not captured |
| BLAKE3 | 261.02 ms | not captured | not captured |

These are Criterion wall-clock numbers only. See [Profiling & energy](/docs/performance/profiling)
to collect RAPL counters.

## MerkleForge vs `rs-merkle` vs `merkle_light`

`cargo bench --bench comparison`

| Metric | MerkleForge | `rs-merkle` | `merkle_light` |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 10K leaf construction | 22.77 ms | 3.69 ms | 2.29 ms |
| Proof size (10K tree) | 469 bytes | 448 bytes | 512 bytes |
| Proof verification | 1.84 µs | 6.39 µs | 1.78 µs |

* Construction uses deterministic 32-byte leaves for all libraries.
* `rs-merkle` receives pre-hashed SHA-256 leaves, matching its public API.
* Proof size is the serialized proof byte count reported by each library.

## Reproduce

```bash
git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge.git
cd MerkleForge

# Everything (long: the Patricia insert group alone can take many minutes)
cargo bench --workspace
xdg-open target/criterion/report/index.html   # `open` on macOS

# Focused groups
cargo bench --bench hash_throughput
cargo bench --bench binary_tree
cargo bench --bench sparse_tree
cargo bench --bench patricia_trie
cargo bench --bench comparison
cargo bench --bench bench_energy

# Print comparative proof sizes
MERKLEFORGE_PRINT_COMPARISON_SIZES=1 cargo bench --bench comparison -- --list
```

Record the machine, kernel, CPU governor, Rust version, and command next to any numbers you
publish. Results are hardware-specific: compare trends across machines, not absolute values.

## Reading the tables

* **Latency:** time for one operation.
* **Throughput:** bytes or elements processed per second.
* **Proof generation:** time to produce the witness sent to a verifier.
* **Proof verification:** time for a stateless client to check the witness against a trusted root.
* **Proof size:** bytes sent over the network or stored as evidence.

# Profiling & energy

Criterion answers *how long did this take?* Profiling answers *where did the CPU time go?* Use the
tools below when investigating construction, proof generation, hashing, memory access, or trie
traversal bottlenecks. All commands run from the repository root.

## Install tools

```bash
make install-profiling-tools
```

On Linux, `cargo-flamegraph` uses `perf`. Depending on your distribution:

```bash
sudo apt install linux-tools-common linux-tools-generic
```

If kernel settings block profiling, lower the restriction temporarily:

```bash
sudo sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid=1
```

## Flamegraphs

```bash
./scripts/flamegraph.sh baseline_construction
```

This writes `flamegraph.svg`. Open it in a browser and inspect the widest frames first; width is
sampled CPU time. Useful targets: `baseline_construction`, `hash_throughput`, `binary_tree`,
`sparse_tree`, `patricia_trie`, `comparison`.

`profiling/flamegraph.svg` in the repository is a reference artifact showing the expected shape.
Regenerate a machine-specific flamegraph before reporting numbers.

## Cache and instruction counters

```bash
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,cache-references \
  cargo bench --bench hash_throughput
```

Per tree:

```bash
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,cache-references cargo bench --bench binary_tree
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,cache-references cargo bench --bench sparse_tree
perf stat -e cycles,instructions,cache-misses,cache-references cargo bench --bench patricia_trie
```

## Energy

The default energy workload builds a 100,000-leaf binary tree with SHA-256, Keccak-256, and BLAKE3.
Criterion measures wall-clock time; Linux `perf` collects CPU package energy externally.

```bash
cargo bench --bench bench_energy   # wall clock → target/criterion/bench_energy/
```

### RAPL counters with `perf`

On Intel and some AMD machines the kernel exposes RAPL counters through the `power/*` PMU. Check
support, then run the helper script:

```bash
perf list 'power/energy-*'
./scripts/energy-perf.sh bench_energy
```

The script collects `power/energy-pkg/` (package Joules), `power/energy-cores/` and
`power/energy-ram/` when available, `cycles`, `instructions`, `cache-references`, `cache-misses`,
and `duration_time`. Some machines need elevated privileges:

```bash
sudo ./scripts/energy-perf.sh bench_energy
# or
sudo sysctl kernel.perf_event_paranoid=0
```

Use the privileged path only on a machine you control. The explicit command behind the script:

```bash
sudo perf stat -a -r 3 \
  -e cycles,instructions,cache-references,cache-misses,duration_time,power/energy-pkg/ \
  -- cargo bench --bench bench_energy
```

`-a` records across all CPUs, which matters because package energy is a socket-level reading.

### Fallbacks

If `perf` doesn't show `power/energy-pkg/`, try `turbostat`:

```bash
sudo turbostat --Summary --Joules --out profiling/turbostat-energy.txt -- \
  cargo bench --bench bench_energy
```

`powertop` is less precise but can capture a repeatable system-level profile while the benchmark
runs in another terminal:

```bash
sudo powertop --time=60 --html=profiling/powertop-energy.html
```

### Interpreting results

* Lower elapsed time: construction finished sooner.
* Lower `power/energy-pkg/` Joules: the CPU package used less energy.
* Fewer cycles for the same workload: less CPU work.
* Cache misses explain why runs with similar hash speed differ in time or energy.

Energy measurements are hardware-specific. Report the machine, kernel, CPU governor, Rust version,
and command line with every table. BLAKE3's lower cycles per byte usually means less energy per
proof, which is why the suite measures all three algorithms.

The full guide lives in
[`benchmarks/ENERGY.md`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/blob/main/benchmarks/ENERGY.md)
and [`profiling/README.md`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/blob/main/profiling/README.md).

# API overview

This page maps the public API of each crate. For full signatures and doc comments, see docs.rs.

| Crate | Import as | docs.rs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `merkle-core` | `merkle_core` | [docs.rs/merkle-core](https://docs.rs/merkle-core) |
| `merkleforge-hash` | `merkleforge_hash` | [docs.rs/merkleforge-hash](https://docs.rs/merkleforge-hash) |
| `merkle-variants` | `merkle_variants` | [docs.rs/merkle-variants](https://docs.rs/merkle-variants) |

:::note
docs.rs shows the latest **published** release (0.4.1). Items marked *Unreleased* below are in the
repository but not yet on crates.io.
:::

## merkle-core

Traits, types, and errors shared by every crate. `no_std` + `alloc` capable
([details](/docs/guides/no-std)).

### `merkle_core::prelude`

Re-exports `MerkleError`, `HashFunction`, `MerkleTree`, `ProofVerifier`, `Serializable`,
`LeafIndex`, `MerkleProof`, `NodeIndex`, `ProofNode`, `ProofSide`, and `TreeMetadata`.

```rust
use merkle_core::prelude::*;

fn main() {
    let index = LeafIndex(3);
    assert_eq!(index.value(), 3);
    assert_eq!(NodeIndex::from(index), NodeIndex(3));
    assert_eq!(NodeIndex::root(4), NodeIndex(6)); // [L0 L1 L2 L3 P01 P23 Root]
}
```

### Traits (`merkle_core::traits`)

| Trait | Methods |
| --- | --- |
| [`HashFunction`](https://docs.rs/merkle-core/latest/merkle_core/traits/hash_function/trait.HashFunction.html) | `type Digest`; `hash`, `algorithm_name`, `digest_size`; provided `hash_nodes`, `hash_encoded_node` (*Unreleased*), `empty` |
| [`MerkleTree<H>`](https://docs.rs/merkle-core/latest/merkle_core/traits/merkle_tree/trait.MerkleTree.html) | `insert`, `remove`, `root`, `leaf_count`, `is_empty`, `height`, `generate_proof`, `metadata` |
| [`ProofVerifier<H>`](https://docs.rs/merkle-core/latest/merkle_core/traits/merkle_tree/trait.ProofVerifier.html) | `verify(expected_root, leaf_data, proof) -> bool` |
| [`Serializable`](https://docs.rs/merkle-core/latest/merkle_core/traits/serializable/trait.Serializable.html) | `to_bytes`, `from_bytes`, `serialized_size`; blanket impl for `Serialize + DeserializeOwned` |

### Types (`merkle_core::types`)

| Type | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `LeafIndex(pub usize)` | Index into the leaf layer. `value()`, `to_node_index()` |
| `NodeIndex(pub usize)` | Index into a flat node array. `value()`, `root(leaf_count)` |
| `ProofSide` | `Left` or `Right`: where the sibling sits |
| `ProofNode<D>` | `hash: D`, `side: ProofSide` |
| `MerkleProof<D>` | `leaf_index`, `leaf_count`, `path: Vec<ProofNode<D>>`; `depth()`, `is_trivial()` |
| `TreeMetadata` | `leaf_count`, `height`, `node_count`, `hash_algorithm`, `variant` |

### Errors (`merkle_core::error`)

`MerkleError`, a `#[non_exhaustive]` enum. See [Errors](/docs/guides/errors).

## merkleforge-hash

| Item | Description |
| --- | --- |
| [`Sha256`](https://docs.rs/merkleforge-hash/latest/merkleforge_hash/struct.Sha256.html) | SHA-256 with `0x00`/`0x01` domain prefixes |
| [`Keccak256`](https://docs.rs/merkleforge-hash/latest/merkleforge_hash/struct.Keccak256.html) | Keccak-256 with `0x00`/`0x01` prefixes; plain Keccak for Patricia nodes |
| [`Blake3`](https://docs.rs/merkleforge-hash/latest/merkleforge_hash/struct.Blake3.html) | BLAKE3 `derive_key` with leaf and internal-node contexts |
| `HashFunction` | Re-export of `merkle_core::traits::HashFunction` |

All three are zero-sized, `Copy`, and produce `[u8; 32]`. See [Hash functions](/docs/guides/hash-functions).

## merkle-variants

Top-level re-exports: `BinaryMerkleTree`, `SparseMerkleTree`, `MerklePatriciaTrie`, `MptProof`.

### `binary` — [`BinaryMerkleTree<H>`](https://docs.rs/merkle-variants/latest/merkle_variants/binary/struct.BinaryMerkleTree.html)

| Method | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `new()`, `with_capacity(n)`, `Default` | Empty tree |
| `from_leaves(iter)` | One-pass `O(n)` build (*Unreleased*) |
| `insert(&[u8]) -> Result<LeafIndex>` | Append a leaf |
| `remove(LeafIndex)` | Replace with `H::empty()` |
| `root()`, `leaf_count()`, `is_empty()`, `height()` | Queries |
| `generate_proof(LeafIndex) -> Result<MerkleProof>` | Inclusion proof |
| `verify(root, leaf, &proof) -> bool` | Stateless, associated function |

Implements `MerkleTree<H>`, `ProofVerifier<H>`; `Clone`, `Debug`, `Serialize`, `Deserialize`
(*Unreleased*). Guide: [Binary Merkle tree](/docs/guides/binary-merkle-tree).

### `sparse` — [`SparseMerkleTree<H>`](https://docs.rs/merkle-variants/latest/merkle_variants/sparse/struct.SparseMerkleTree.html)

| Method | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `new()`, `Default` | Empty 256-depth tree |
| `insert(key, &[u8])`, `batch_insert(&[(key, Vec<u8>)])` | Insert or overwrite |
| `remove(key)`, `batch_remove(&[key])` | Remove existing keys |
| `get(key) -> Option<&Digest>` | Stored leaf hash |
| `generate_membership_proof(key) -> Result<SparseMerkleProof>` | Membership or non-membership |
| `verify_membership(root, key, leaf, &proof)` | Checks key, value, path (*Unreleased*) |
| `verify_non_membership(root, key, &proof)` | Absence proof |
| `verify(root, leaf, &proof)` | **Deprecated**: doesn't check the key |
| `root()`, `empty_root()`, `leaf_count()`, `is_empty()`, `height()`, `depth()` | Queries |
| `empty_hash_at(level)`, `empty_hashes()` | Empty-subtree cache |
| `stored_node_count()`, `last_node_access_count()`, `unbatched_node_count_estimate()` | Storage introspection |

Also: `SparseMerkleProof<D>` (`key`, `siblings`, `leaf`; `is_membership()`,
`is_non_membership()`), `NodeEntry<D>` (with `commitment()`, *Unreleased*), `SubtreeBatch<D>`,
`bit_at`, and the constants `SPARSE_TREE_DEPTH`, `EMPTY_HASH_LEVELS`, `BATCH_DEPTH`. Guide:
[Sparse Merkle tree](/docs/guides/sparse-merkle-tree).

### `patricia` — [`MerklePatriciaTrie<H>`](https://docs.rs/merkle-variants/latest/merkle_variants/patricia/struct.MerklePatriciaTrie.html)

| Method | Notes |
| --- | --- |
| `new()`, `Default` | Empty trie |
| `insert(key, value)`, `remove(key)`, `get(key) -> Option<&[u8]>` | Key-value operations |
| `generate_proof(key) -> Result<MptProof>` | RLP witness, membership or non-membership |
| `verify_proof(root, &proof) -> bool` | Stateless |
| `root()`, `is_empty()`, `leaf_count()`, `node_count()`, `height()` | Queries |

Also: `MptProof<D>` (`key`, `value`, `proof_nodes`; `new`, `is_membership`, `is_non_membership`),
`MptNode<D>`, `NodeRef<D>`, `NibblePath`, `hp_encode`, `hp_decode`, `rlp_encode`, `rlp_decode`,
`hash_node`, `compute_root_hash`. Guide: [Merkle Patricia trie](/docs/guides/merkle-patricia-trie).

## Safety

Every published crate uses `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` and `#![deny(missing_docs)]`.

# Changelog

The full changelog lives in the repository:
**[CHANGELOG.md on GitHub](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/blob/main/CHANGELOG.md)**.

`merkle-core`, `merkleforge-hash`, and `merkle-variants` are versioned together; one entry covers
all published crates. `merkle-bench` is never published. The project follows
[Keep a Changelog](https://keepachangelog.com/en/1.1.0/) and
[Semantic Versioning](https://semver.org/spec/v2.0.0.html).

## Highlights

### Unreleased

Correctness and performance fixes. Roots and proofs for the shipped hash adapters are unchanged.

* **Added:** `BinaryMerkleTree::from_leaves` (one-pass `O(n)` build),
  `SparseMerkleTree::verify_membership` (checks the proof's key),
  `HashFunction::hash_encoded_node`, `NodeEntry::commitment`, and `Clone` / `Debug` / `Serialize` /
  `Deserialize` for all three trees.
* **Fixed:** sparse and Patricia inserts and removals recompute only the changed path (4,000
  sparse inserts: about 223 s to 0.2 s; one sparse proof: 151 ms to 25 µs; 4,000 Patricia inserts:
  about 5.9 s to 0.02 s). `MerkleTree::insert` on sparse and Patricia trees no longer overwrites a
  leaf after a removal.
* **Breaking:** the default `HashFunction::hash_nodes` now hashes `0x01 ‖ left ‖ right`;
  `MerklePatriciaTrie` selects plain Keccak through `hash_encoded_node` instead of the algorithm
  name; the hidden `MptNode::__DigestMarker` variant is gone.
* **Deprecated:** `SparseMerkleTree::verify`. Use `verify_membership`.

### 0.4.1 (2026-09-05)

Packaging and documentation refresh for the MerkleForge Framework rebrand: crate metadata,
rewritten crate READMEs, and `CONTRIBUTING.md`.

### 0.4.0 (2026-07-27)

Adds the Ethereum-compatible `MerklePatriciaTrie<H>` with RLP and hex-prefix encoding,
EIP-1186-style `MptProof` witnesses, and validation against official Ethereum trie vectors.

# Security

## Audit status

:::warning
**MerkleForge has not completed an independent security audit.**

The codebase is tested with unit, integration, property-based, benchmark, and Ethereum
test-vector tests, but tests are not an audit. Review the code, your threat model, and the test
coverage before using MerkleForge in production systems, financial applications, or other
security-critical environments.
:::

## Reporting a vulnerability

Please **do not** report vulnerabilities in public issues.

1. Open the **Security** tab of the
   [repository](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/security) and click
   **Report a vulnerability** to use GitHub Security Advisories.
2. Or email the details to [dicethedev@gmail.com](mailto\:dicethedev@gmail.com).

Include as much as you can:

* a clear description of the issue;
* steps to reproduce, ideally with proof-of-concept code;
* affected versions or components;
* potential impact and severity, and whether you believe it is being actively exploited.

Don't disclose publicly until the issue is confirmed and fixed, and don't access, modify, or destroy
data that isn't yours. The maintainers will acknowledge and investigate reports, may contact you
for details, and will coordinate disclosure once a fix is available.

There is no formal bug bounty. With your consent, your contribution may be credited in the
changelog or release notes.

The canonical policy is
[`.github/SECURITY.md`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/blob/main/.github/SECURITY.md).

## Design properties

* `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` in every published crate.
* **Domain separation** between leaves (`0x00`) and internal nodes (`0x01`), or BLAKE3 context
  strings, to prevent second-preimage attacks. See [Mental model](/docs/mental-model#domain-separation-0x00-and-0x01).
* **Empty leaves rejected** so inserted data can't be confused with padding.
* **Verifiers never panic** on malformed proofs; they return `false`.
* **Deserialization rebuilds** internal nodes from leaves and rejects data from another hash
  algorithm, so a decoded tree is always internally consistent.

## What integrators must get right

* **Trust the root, not the prover.** A proof shows consistency with a root; it says nothing about
  whether that root is the right one.
* **`MerkleProof::leaf_count` is not committed** by the binary root. Obtain it independently if it
  matters.
* **Check the key** on sparse proofs with `verify_membership`. The deprecated
  `SparseMerkleTree::verify` accepts a valid proof for *any* key holding the value.
* **Canonical leaf encoding.** Prover and verifier must hash exactly the same bytes.
* **Custom hash adapters** must keep leaf and node domains separate. Since *Unreleased*, the default
  `hash_nodes` applies the `0x01` prefix for you. See
  [Hash functions](/docs/guides/hash-functions#writing-a-custom-adapter).

# Brand assets

The MerkleForge mark is the **Forged block**: a solid rounded block with a Merkle root and two
branches cut out of it. It reads as a tree, an anvil-struck block, and a sealed hash at once.

<BrandPreview />

## Files

All assets live in
[`assets/brand/`](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/tree/main/assets/brand) in the
repository. Wordmark text is converted to outlines, so the SVGs need no fonts.

| Folder | What | Use it for |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `svg/mark/`, `png/mark/` | Mark alone, black or white, transparent cut-outs (64–1024 px) | Avatars, docs headers, small spaces |
| `svg/lockup/`, `png/lockup/` | Mark + wordmark, horizontal and stacked | README, website header, slides |
| `svg/wordmark/`, `png/wordmark/` | Wordmark only | Where the mark already appears nearby |
| `svg/icon/`, `png/icon/` | App icon (dark/light, 1024) and avatar (512/1024) | GitHub org, crates.io, X, Discord |
| `favicon/` | `favicon.svg` (adapts to dark mode), `.ico`, 16/32/48 PNG, apple-touch, 192/512, `site.webmanifest` | Website and docs |
| `svg/banner/`, `png/banner/` | GitHub social preview, README, X header, LinkedIn (dark + light) | Social and repository cards |

## Colour

Monochrome by design: black, white, and a short grey ramp. **No accent colour.**

<BrandSwatches />

| Name | Hex | Role |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Forge Black | `#000000` | Primary ground, mark on light |
| Ink | `#141414` | Raised surfaces, ghost mark in banners |
| Steel | `#262626` | Borders, dividers on dark |
| Graphite | `#6B6B6B` | Secondary text on light, large only on dark |
| Slate | `#5C5C5C` | "Forge" in the wordmark on light |
| Ash | `#A3A3A3` | "Forge" in the wordmark on dark, captions on dark |
| White | `#FFFFFF` | Mark on dark, primary text on dark |

## Type

* **Space Grotesk**: wordmark (Merkle 700 / Forge 400, tracking −3%), headings 500–700.
* **JetBrains Mono**: code, hashes, technical labels (400–500).

Both are free on Google Fonts under the SIL Open Font License.

## Usage

* **Clear space:** keep at least ¼ of the mark's height empty on every side.
* **Minimum size:** mark 16 px; horizontal lockup 24 px tall.
* Use the black mark on light grounds and the white mark on dark grounds.
* Don't recolour, rotate, outline, stretch, add shadows or gradients, or rearrange the mark and
  wordmark.
* Don't place the mark on busy photos; use a solid black or white panel.
