# Contributing

Contributions are welcome across correctness, documentation, benchmarks, examples, developer
experience, and performance analysis. By participating, you agree to follow the
[Code of Conduct](/docs/community/code-of-conduct).

## Good first contributions

* Improve docs, Rustdoc, examples, or these pages (every page has a *Suggest changes* link).
* Add benchmark reproduction notes for different hardware.
* Add test vectors for Binary, Sparse, or Patricia trees.
* Improve error messages or API examples.
* Investigate performance with Criterion, `perf`, or flamegraphs.

## Development setup

```bash
git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge.git
cd MerkleForge
cargo test --workspace
```

The workspace pins Rust 1.97.1 in `rust-toolchain.toml`; `rustup` installs it automatically.

For work on this website (in `docs/`, built with [Vocs](https://vocs.dev)):

```bash
cd docs
npm ci
npm run dev
```

## Recommended workflow

1. Open or comment on an issue first for large API, storage, or cryptography changes.
2. Create a focused branch, for example `fix/docs-links` or `feat/sparse-proof-tests`.
3. Keep the pull request small enough to review comfortably.
4. Add or update tests for behaviour changes.
5. Update docs when public APIs, examples, or benchmark behaviour change.

## Required checks

Run these before opening a pull request:

```bash
make fmt    # rustfmt
make lint   # Clippy across the workspace, warnings denied
make test   # all workspace tests in release mode
```

For website changes, also run:

```bash
npm --prefix docs run build
```

## Pull request guidelines

* Explain the problem, the change, and how you verified it.
* Link related issues.
* Keep `target/`, local benchmark noise, editor files, and temporary artifacts out of commits.
* Include benchmark numbers only with the environment and command recorded.
* Avoid unrelated refactors in feature or bug-fix pull requests.

## Security

Don't report vulnerabilities in public issues. Follow the disclosure process on the
[Security](/docs/reference/security) page.

# Code of Conduct

## Our Pledge

We as members, contributors, and leaders pledge to make participation in the
MerkleForge community a harassment-free experience for everyone, regardless of
age, body size, visible or invisible disability, ethnicity, sex
characteristics, gender identity and expression, level of experience,
education, socio-economic status, nationality, personal appearance, race,
caste, color, religion, or sexual identity and orientation.

We pledge to act and interact in ways that contribute to an open, welcoming,
diverse, inclusive, and healthy community.

## Our Standards

Examples of behavior that contributes to a positive environment for our
community include:

* Demonstrating empathy and kindness toward other people
* Being respectful of differing opinions, viewpoints, and experiences
* Giving and gracefully accepting constructive feedback
* Accepting responsibility and apologizing to those affected by our mistakes,
  and learning from the experience
* Focusing on what is best not just for us as individuals, but for the overall
  community

Examples of unacceptable behavior include:

* The use of sexualized language or imagery, and sexual attention or advances
  of any kind
* Trolling, insulting or derogatory comments, and personal or political attacks
* Public or private harassment
* Publishing others' private information, such as a physical or email address,
  without their explicit permission
* Other conduct which could reasonably be considered inappropriate in a
  professional setting

## Enforcement Responsibilities

Community leaders are responsible for clarifying and enforcing our standards of
acceptable behavior and will take appropriate and fair corrective action in
response to any behavior that they deem inappropriate, threatening, offensive,
or harmful.

Community leaders have the right and responsibility to remove, edit, or reject
comments, commits, code, wiki edits, issues, and other contributions that are
not aligned to this Code of Conduct, and will communicate reasons for
moderation decisions when appropriate.

## Scope

This Code of Conduct applies within all community spaces, including the
MerkleForge repository, issues, pull requests, discussions, and project chat
channels, and also applies when an individual is officially representing the
community in public spaces. Examples of representing our community include
using an official email address, posting via an official social media account,
or acting as an appointed representative at an online or offline event.

## Reporting

Instances of abusive, harassing, or otherwise unacceptable behavior may be
reported to the project maintainers at
[dicethedev@gmail.com](mailto\:dicethedev@gmail.com). All complaints will be
reviewed and investigated promptly and fairly.

All community leaders are obligated to respect the privacy and security of the
reporter of any incident.

Security vulnerabilities are not Code of Conduct matters. Please report them
through the process in the [security policy](/docs/reference/security).

## Enforcement Guidelines

Community leaders will follow these Community Impact Guidelines in determining
the consequences for any action they deem in violation of this Code of Conduct:

### 1. Correction

**Community Impact**: Use of inappropriate language or other behavior deemed
unprofessional or unwelcome in the community.

**Consequence**: A private, written warning from community leaders, providing
clarity around the nature of the violation and an explanation of why the
behavior was inappropriate. A public apology may be requested.

### 2. Warning

**Community Impact**: A violation through a single incident or series of
actions.

**Consequence**: A warning with consequences for continued behavior. No
interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction with
those enforcing the Code of Conduct, for a specified period of time. This
includes avoiding interactions in community spaces as well as external channels
like social media. Violating these terms may lead to a temporary or permanent
ban.

### 3. Temporary Ban

**Community Impact**: A serious violation of community standards, including
sustained inappropriate behavior.

**Consequence**: A temporary ban from any sort of interaction or public
communication with the community for a specified period of time. No public or
private interaction with the people involved, including unsolicited interaction
with those enforcing the Code of Conduct, is allowed during this period.
Violating these terms may lead to a permanent ban.

### 4. Permanent Ban

**Community Impact**: Demonstrating a pattern of violation of community
standards, including sustained inappropriate behavior, harassment of an
individual, or aggression toward or disparagement of classes of individuals.

**Consequence**: A permanent ban from any sort of public interaction within the
community.

## Attribution

This Code of Conduct is adapted from the [Contributor Covenant][homepage],
version 2.1, available at
[https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/version/2/1/code_of_conduct.html).

Community Impact Guidelines were inspired by
[Mozilla's code of conduct enforcement ladder][mozilla coc].

For answers to common questions about this code of conduct, see the FAQ at
[https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/faq). Translations are available at
[https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations](https://www.contributor-covenant.org/translations).

[mozilla coc]: https://github.com/mozilla/diversity

# Projects using MerkleForge

## ProofStream

ProofStream turns live indexed DEX activity into portable proof receipts. It normalizes blockchain
records into deterministic rows, commits them with a MerkleForge `BinaryMerkleTree<Keccak256>`,
and lets a browser verify one selected activity using only the row, its compact proof, and the
dataset root.

* [ProofStream repository](https://github.com/dicethedev/ProofStream)
* [ETHGlobal Online 2026 showcase](https://ethglobal.com/showcase/proofstream-jvup1)

## Add your project

Building something with MerkleForge? Open a pull request that adds a short section to
[this page](https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge/edit/main/docs/pages/docs/community/projects.mdx)
with a one-paragraph description and links.

        :::
      </div>

      ```rust [src/main.rs]
      use merkle_core::prelude::*;
      use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;

      fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
          let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves([
              "alice:100", "bob:250", "carol:75",
          ])?;

          let root = tree.root().expect("tree is non-empty");
          let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(1))?;

          // Stateless: only the root, the leaf bytes, and the proof.
          assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(root, b"bob:250", &proof));
          Ok(())
      }
      ```

<div className="mf-page" style={{ paddingTop: 0 }}>
  # Benchmarks

  Criterion results from the latest site build, across tree variants, operations, hash adapters, and
  sizes. Every row links to its full Criterion report. Lower is better.

  <BenchmarkExplorer />

  ## MerkleForge vs `rs-merkle` vs `merkle_light`

  From the published comparison run (`cargo bench --bench comparison`, i7-1185G7, 2026-08-17):

  | Metric | MerkleForge | `rs-merkle` | `merkle_light` |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 10K leaf construction | 22.77 ms | 3.69 ms | 2.29 ms |
  | Proof size (10K tree) | 469 bytes | 448 bytes | 512 bytes |
  | Proof verification | 1.84 µs | 6.39 µs | 1.78 µs |

  Construction uses deterministic 32-byte leaves for every library; `rs-merkle` receives pre-hashed
  SHA-256 leaves, matching its API. Proof size is each library's serialized proof byte count.

  ## Reproduce

  ```bash
  git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge.git
  cd MerkleForge

  cargo bench --workspace
  xdg-open target/criterion/report/index.html   # `open` on macOS

  # Focused groups
  cargo bench --bench hash_throughput
  cargo bench --bench binary_tree
  cargo bench --bench sparse_tree
  cargo bench --bench patricia_trie
  cargo bench --bench comparison
  cargo bench --bench bench_energy

  # Comparative proof sizes
  MERKLEFORGE_PRINT_COMPARISON_SIZES=1 cargo bench --bench comparison -- --list
  ```

  The full published tables, environment, and caveats are on the
  [Benchmarks docs page](/docs/performance/benchmarks). To profile hotspots or measure energy, see
  [Profiling & energy](/docs/performance/profiling).
</div>

<div className="mf-page" style={{ paddingTop: 0 }}>
  # Light-client demo

  A server commits rows to a Merkle root and sends one row plus its proof to a client. The client
  holds only the trusted root. Edit the rows, pick one to prove, then change the **claimed value** to
  see tampering rejected.

  The browser mirrors `BinaryMerkleTree<Sha256>` with WebCrypto: leaves are
  `SHA-256(0x00 ‖ row)`, internal nodes `SHA-256(0x01 ‖ left ‖ right)`, and the leaf layer is padded
  to a power of two with `Sha256::empty()`. Roots match the Rust crate for the same rows.

  <LightClientDemo />

  ## The same flow in Rust

  ```rust [merkle-variants/examples/light_client.rs]
  use merkle_core::{error::MerkleError, types::LeafIndex};
  use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
  use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

  fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
      let proof;
      let root;

      {
          let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
          tree.insert(b"tx:alice->bob:100")?;
          tree.insert(b"tx:bob->carol:50")?;
          tree.insert(b"tx:carol->dave:25")?;

          root = *tree.root().expect("tree has inserted leaves");
          proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(0))?;

          println!("server: built tree and exported root + proof");
      }

      let valid = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(&root, b"tx:alice->bob:100", &proof);

      println!("client: tree dropped before verification");
      println!("Stateless verification: {valid}");

      Ok(())
  }
  ```

  ```bash
  git clone https://github.com/1888-Labs/MerkleForge.git
  cd MerkleForge
  cargo run -p merkle-variants --example light_client
  ```

  ```text
  server: built tree and exported root + proof
  client: tree dropped before verification
  Stateless verification: true
  ```

  Learn more in [Proofs & stateless verification](/docs/guides/proofs).
</div>

# Examples

Complete programs you can paste into `src/main.rs`. Each one compiles against the current
crates; add the dependencies first:

```toml [Cargo.toml]
[dependencies]
merkle-core = "0.4.1"
merkleforge-hash = "0.4.1"
merkle-variants = "0.4.1"
```

:::note
Examples that use `BinaryMerkleTree::from_leaves` or tree serialization need the current
repository version (listed as **Unreleased** in the changelog). Everything else works with 0.4.1.
:::

## Binary inclusion proof

Build a tree, prove one leaf, and verify it with only the root, the proof, and the leaf bytes.
[Guide](/docs/guides/binary-merkle-tree)

```rust [src/main.rs]
use merkle_core::types::LeafIndex;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
    tree.insert(b"alice:100")?;
    tree.insert(b"bob:250")?;

    let proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(0))?;
    let root = tree.root().expect("tree is not empty");

    assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(
        root,
        b"alice:100",
        &proof,
    ));
    Ok(())
}
```

## Sparse account state

Commit balances under 32-byte keys and prove one account's value.
[Guide](/docs/guides/sparse-merkle-tree)

```rust [src/main.rs]
use merkle_variants::SparseMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    let mut state = SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
    let alice = [7_u8; 32];
    let bob = [9_u8; 32];

    state.insert(alice, b"balance:100")?;
    state.insert(bob, b"balance:250")?;

    let proof = state.generate_membership_proof(alice)?;
    let root = state.root().expect("state is not empty");

    assert!(SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_membership(
        root,
        alice,
        b"balance:100",
        &proof,
    ));

    // Prove that a key is absent.
    let carol = [11_u8; 32];
    let absent = state.generate_membership_proof(carol)?;
    assert!(SparseMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify_non_membership(root, carol, &absent));
    Ok(())
}
```

## Patricia witness

Ethereum-style key-value state with an RLP witness. [Guide](/docs/guides/merkle-patricia-trie)

```rust [src/main.rs]
use merkle_variants::MerklePatriciaTrie;
use merkleforge_hash::Keccak256;

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    let mut trie = MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::new();

    trie.insert(b"account:alice", b"100")?;
    trie.insert(b"account:bob", b"250")?;

    let proof = trie.generate_proof(b"account:alice")?;
    let root = trie.root().expect("trie is not empty");

    assert_eq!(proof.key, b"account:alice");
    assert_eq!(proof.value.as_deref(), Some(b"100".as_slice()));
    println!("witness has {} RLP nodes", proof.proof_nodes.len());
    assert!(MerklePatriciaTrie::<Keccak256>::verify_proof(root, &proof));
    Ok(())
}
```

## Swap the hash function

The same tree API over three algorithms. [Guide](/docs/guides/hash-functions)

```rust [src/main.rs]
use merkle_core::traits::MerkleTree;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::{Blake3, Keccak256, Sha256};

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    let mut sha_tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
    let mut eth_tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Keccak256>::new();
    let mut fast_tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Blake3>::new();

    for leaf in [b"alice".as_slice(), b"bob", b"carol"] {
        sha_tree.insert(leaf)?;
        eth_tree.insert(leaf)?;
        fast_tree.insert(leaf)?;
    }

    for meta in [sha_tree.metadata(), eth_tree.metadata(), fast_tree.metadata()] {
        println!("{}: {} leaves, height {}", meta.hash_algorithm, meta.leaf_count, meta.height);
    }
    Ok(())
}
```

## Hash directly

Use an adapter without a tree: leaf hashes, parent hashes, and metadata.

```rust [src/main.rs]
use merkle_core::traits::HashFunction;
use merkleforge_hash::Blake3;

fn main() {
    let left = Blake3::hash(b"left leaf");
    let right = Blake3::hash(b"right leaf");
    let parent = Blake3::hash_nodes(&left, &right);

    assert_ne!(parent, left);
    assert_eq!(Blake3::digest_size(), 32);
    assert_eq!(Blake3::algorithm_name(), "BLAKE3");
}
```

## Tree metadata

Inspect a tree for logs and dashboards. [Guide](/docs/guides/metadata)

```rust [src/main.rs]
use merkle_core::traits::MerkleTree;
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(["alice", "bob", "carol"])?;

    let metadata = tree.metadata();
    println!("variant: {}", metadata.variant);
    println!("algorithm: {}", metadata.hash_algorithm);
    println!("leaves: {}", metadata.leaf_count);
    println!("height: {}", metadata.height);
    println!("allocated nodes: {}", metadata.node_count);
    Ok(())
}
```

## Proof transport

Serialize a proof to bytes on the server and decode it on the client.
[Guide](/docs/guides/serialization)

```rust [src/main.rs]
use merkle_core::{
    traits::Serializable,
    types::{LeafIndex, MerkleProof},
};
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), merkle_core::error::MerkleError> {
    // Server
    let tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::from_leaves(["tx1", "tx2", "tx3"])?;
    let root = *tree.root().expect("tree is not empty");
    let bytes = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(1))?.to_bytes()?;

    // ... send `root` (trusted channel) and `bytes` (any channel) ...

    // Client
    let proof = MerkleProof::<[u8; 32]>::from_bytes(&bytes)?;
    assert!(BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(&root, b"tx2", &proof));
    Ok(())
}
```

## Stateless light client

The repository's runnable example: the tree is dropped before verification.

```rust [merkle-variants/examples/light_client.rs]
use merkle_core::{error::MerkleError, types::LeafIndex};
use merkle_variants::BinaryMerkleTree;
use merkleforge_hash::Sha256;

fn main() -> Result<(), MerkleError> {
    let proof;
    let root;

    {
        let mut tree = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::new();
        tree.insert(b"tx:alice->bob:100")?;
        tree.insert(b"tx:bob->carol:50")?;
        tree.insert(b"tx:carol->dave:25")?;

        root = *tree.root().expect("tree has inserted leaves");
        proof = tree.generate_proof(LeafIndex(0))?;

        println!("server: built tree and exported root + proof");
    }

    let valid = BinaryMerkleTree::<Sha256>::verify(&root, b"tx:alice->bob:100", &proof);

    println!("client: tree dropped before verification");
    println!("Stateless verification: {valid}");

    Ok(())
}
```

```bash
cargo run -p merkle-variants --example light_client
```

See it in the browser on the [live demo](/demo).
